title: What this means for energy traders — Saturday, November 7, 2026

sections.overall: The week's news was driven by two forces: the Iran conflict, which dominated crude and refined-product coverage, and a steady stream of long-term LNG contracting. Oil moved on diplomacy headlines around the US midterms, while gas-market stories were more structural: supply deals, project milestones and storage worries in Europe. Both confirmed trends in the ledger are rated STEADY, so today's evidence is continuity rather than acceleration.
sections.CRUDE_OIL: Coverage described a sharp weekly decline after the midterms, with investors weighing the risk of renewed Iran escalation against prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough (CNBC). Crude was reported below $90 a barrel midweek (CNBC). A Bloomberg survey, reported by Rigzone, said OPEC output neared pre-war levels as Gulf supply recovered (Rigzone). Headline sensitivity to diplomacy is high, and it is still unclear how durable the supply recovery is given continued attacks on regional infrastructure.
sections.NATURAL_GAS: LNG contracting continues: ADNOC and TotalEnergies both signed Asian-linked deals this week (LNG Prime, LNG Prime). Long-dated contracts of this kind are generally read as signalling buyer concern about security of supply. Germany missing its winter storage target (Financial Times) and rising Atlantic and Pacific spot shipping rates (LNG Prime) point to tightness in the near-term market. Also unclear: how much of the contracting reflects binding volumes versus preliminary heads of agreement.
sections.REFINED_PRODUCTS: Refinery yields have shifted toward middle distillates on strong margins (EIA). US fuel supplies were reported at a 20-year low while a diesel arrangement with Russia faltered (Financial Times), and Ukraine struck a sixth Russian refinery in a week (Rigzone). Airlines such as Qantas are citing fuel costs in fare plans. Supply-side disruption and a distillate-heavy slate are the main threads.
sections.CARBON_CREDITS: Verra reported its first credits under a CCS methodology and the first ICVCM approval for coal-retirement transition credits, which are methodology milestones for the voluntary market (Verra, Verra). In compliance markets, EUAs posted their largest weekly fall in five months while RGGI rose 6% on short covering (Carbon Pulse, Carbon Pulse). A leaked Council document showed EU states split over the post-2030 cap trajectory (Carbon Pulse). Corporate removal purchasing had no new deals in today's digest.
